sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Texas, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Friday, October 23Passed

Your application must be received (not just postmarked) by your county's Early Voting Clerk by Friday, October 23, 2026, by the close of regular business or 12 noon, whichever is later. (The rule: the 11th day before Election Day.) (official page)

Send it back

Received by the Early Voting Clerk by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026; or, if mailed inside the United States with a postmark showing it was mailed by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, received by 5:00 p.m. on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Friday, October 30, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Texas’s own page on voting by mail

At school away from home, in Texas or in another state? What Texas says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

Yes. You may vote by mail only if you: will be away from your county on Election Day and during the early voting hours; are sick or disabled; expect to give birth within three weeks before or after Election Day; are 65 or older on Election Day; or are confined in jail or under involuntary civil commitment. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • By mail. Fill in the Application for a Ballot by Mail (download it, or ask the Secretary of State's office or your county's Early Voting Clerk for one) and send it to the Early Voting Clerk in the county where you are registered. Applications sent to any other address may be rejected. Texas lists no way to apply online. Open it (official page)
  • Email or fax. You may email a signed, scanned application, or fax it if the clerk's office has a fax. If you do, you must also mail the original so the clerk receives it by the fourth business day after the email or fax. (official page)
  • In person. You may hand the application to the Early Voting Clerk. If you are voting by mail because you will be away, you may apply in person before early voting in person begins. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail the signed carrier envelope to your county's Early Voting Clerk, or send it by a delivery company. The state warns that some mail is not postmarked on the day it is collected, so send it back as soon as you can. (official page)
  • In person. Deliver it in person on Election Day at your county Early Voting Clerk's office. (official page)
  • Someone else for you. If someone helps you mark or mail your ballot, their name and address must be written on the carrier envelope and they must sign it. A ballot delivered by a delivery company from the address of a candidate or a campaign headquarters is rejected. (official page)

What the envelope needs

Both the application and the carrier envelope must carry ONE of these numbers: your Texas driver license, Texas personal ID card or Election Identification Certificate number (not your voter registration VUID number); or, if you have none of those, the last 4 digits of your Social Security number; or a checked box saying you have none. Seal and sign the carrier envelope. If someone helps you, their name and address go on the envelope and they sign too. (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Texas’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Monday, October 19, 2026 to Friday, October 30, 2026.

Early voting in person for the November 3, 2026 election runs October 19 through October 30, 2026. (official page)

Students

At school in Texas, away from home

The state's pages do not speak to students separately; its general rule is the Election Code's meaning of residence: your home is the place you intend to return to after any temporary absence. You do not lose your residence by leaving for temporary purposes only, and you do not gain a new one in a place you came to only for a while without meaning to make it your home. You may not claim a place you have not lived in. Being away from your home county on Election Day and during early voting is one of the reasons Texas allows for voting by mail (see who can vote by mail above); then the ballot is mailed to an address outside the county. (the law)

At school in another state, with Texas as home

The state's pages do not speak to students at school in another state separately. Under the Election Code's residence rule you do not lose your Texas residence by leaving for temporary purposes only. Being away from your county on Election Day and during early voting is a reason to vote by mail, and the ballot is then mailed to an address outside your county. A student living outside the United States may use the federal FPCA form as an overseas voter. (the law)

Military and overseas

Send the federal FPCA form to your county Early Voting Clerk by the 11th day before Election Day (October 23, 2026); you can get your blank ballot by email. A ballot mailed from overseas must be postmarked by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day and received by the fifth day after Election Day. A military voter who used the FPCA has until the sixth day after, with no postmark needed. This year the fifth day is Sunday, November 8, and a deadline on a weekend moves to the next business day, so both come out to Monday, November 9, 2026. (official page)

Texas in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • A voter who is 65 or older or disabled can mark one 'annual' application to get mail ballots for every election in the calendar year.
  • If your application or envelope is missing an ID number, or the number does not match your record, you can fix it online in the Ballot by Mail Tracker, or by sending a new application.
  • Texas's official statute website did not show the text of Section 1.015 to a request on 2026-10-21, so the residence rule is taken from the Secretary of State's advisory, which quotes the section in full.
Where this comes from: 7 pages of Texas’s election office, its laws and the federal guide

  2. Application for a Ballot by Mail (ABBM), Texas Secretary of State (VoteTexas.gov) (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  3. Completing and Mailing your Carrier Envelope, Texas Secretary of State (VoteTexas.gov) (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  4. Track your Ballot by Mail, Texas Secretary of State (VoteTexas.gov) (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  5. Election notice at the top of the Secretary of State's pages: early voting for the November 3 election runs Oct. 19-30; mail ballot applications must be received by Oct. 23, Texas Secretary of State (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  6. Texas Election Code Sec. 1.015, Residence (quoted in full in Election Advisory No. 2021-10), Texas Secretary of State (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  7. Military & Overseas Voters, Texas Secretary of State (VoteTexas.gov) (official page; read October 21, 2026)

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: Texas’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.

polls:
Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. (source)

  • rest of the state: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. CST
  • Far West Texas: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. MST

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
